---
title: 1 - Setup
---

## 1.1. Install required software

You will need the following software:

- **Visual Studio Code (VS Code)** or another code editor of your choice.
- **Node.js** (14 or higher), which includes npm, the package manager used to install project dependencies.
- **Git**, which is useful for version control and working with GitHub.

Install the lat4est version of Node.js from [the official Node.js website](https://nodejs.org/en). Install Git from [the Git website](https://git-scm.com/install).

This tutorial uses Visual Studio Code, but most code editors provide the same functionalities. The screenshots therefore show VS Code interfave, and the layout may differ if you use another editor. No extensions are used in this tutorial, but if you like to use any, feel free to use them as you like.



## 1.2. Create a working folder

Create a folder on your computer for your webmap project. You can call it `webmap` or choose another name. Cloud locations work too.

Open the code editing software and open the empty webmap folder in there. Usually by **File → Open Folder...**. Navigate to your new folder and open it.

You will use this folder to store the webmap code and geospatial data files displayed on the map.

[*Open a working folder in VS Code*](images/1-2_open-folder.png)



## 1.3. Set up the OpenLayers application

Follow the [OpenLayers Quick Start guide](https://openlayers.org/doc/quickstart.html) to create a basic OpenLayers application and the required file structure in your working folder.

Open a terminal in your code editing software, often via **Terminal → New Terminal**. Make sure the terminal is working in your project folder before running the commands in the Quick Start guide (the terminal path should end with *...\webmap*). If everything is fine, run the commands in the exact order.

The setup creates the files and installs the dependencies needed to run the application. We will build on this starting point throughout the tutorial.

After you run `npm start`, you may be prompted with action suggestions. Feel free to run those, but often they are not a necessity for the OpenLayers application to run. 

If everything goes well, the terminal will display a local development server address, typically `http://localhost:5173/`. Open this address in your browser to view the default webmap.

!The development server allows you to test your changes locally while you work. The map is not yet published online.!

*Screenshot 2: VS Code terminal showing the development server running and the local address WITH a screenshot of the blank OSM basemap of the world.*



## 1.4. Explore the project files

Take a moment to explore the files created by the setup.

- `index.html` defines the basic structure of the web page and provides a container for the map.
- `main.js` contains the JavaScript code that creates and configures the map.
- `style.css` controls the appearance and layout of the page and map.

Each of the files above already contain some code, so you won't have to start from scratch. Once you open the local development server URL in your browser (or code editing software), you should see a basic OpenStreetMap basemap.

**Important:** Do not open `index.html` directly from your file system as your main way of testing the map. Use the local development server instead. Some web resources and JavaScript modules require a server, and direct file access can cause errors. The OpenStreetMap tile service also has usage policies, so avoid unnecessary requests to its servers.

*However, you will most likely encounter a bunch of blocked OSM tiles with a warning. This is due to OSM server usage policies to prevent exessive usage of their volunteer-run servers. The OSM tiles will be visible when publishing the webmap, but a bit annoying to look at them in the development stage. Thus, using a local server is recommended to avoid the warnings and actually display the webmap. Read more about OSM policies: [the link to the osm wiki blocked]. *

*Screenshot 3: The initial webmap displayed in a browser, with the local address visible.*


### Checkpoint

Before continuing, make sure that:

- The project folder is open in your code editor.
- The development server starts without errors.
- The local webmap opens in your browser and displays a basemap.

If the map does not appear, check the terminal for error messages before proceeding.
